extracted.intended_audience: regulated parties, agency staff, administrative-law practitioners, and members of the public interested in interim final rules and notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and document-level practices concerning the issuance, correction, adoption/rescission, effective dates, and public-participation procedures for interim final rules (IFRs) in U.S. federal rulemaking. Useful for evaluating when IFRs are justified, how agencies solicit and handle comments, and procedural obligations (e.g., CRA/OIRA, APA §553).

rubrics_metrics.name: Good cause to issue rule without advance notice-and-comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency may find 'good cause' to issue an interim final rule without advance notice-and-comment and with an immediate effective date when notice-and-comment is unnecessary or impracticable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and language from page: "The Board has found good cause to issue the interim final rule without advance notice-and-comment procedures and with an immediate effective date." Also: "good cause exists to make notice and comment unnecessary." Common justifications include corrections, technical or minor changes, or other circumstances where delay would be impracticable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interim final rule satisfies APA-required elements for an NPRM
rubrics_metrics.description: An IFR that contains all elements required by the Administrative Procedure Act for a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) may be treated as satisfying the APA's procedural requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verbatim/near-verbatim: "An interim final rule containing all elements required by the APA for an NPRM, as provided in 5 U.S.C. 553(b)-(d), satisfies the APA's procedural requirements." Agencies rely on this to justify use of IFR mechanism to effect changes while accepting comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate effectiveness under APA section 553(d) when rule relieves obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency may make a final or interim final rule effective immediately under APA §553(d) when the rule 'relieves obligations' or 'relieves a restriction', obviating need for delayed effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From EPA example: "cause for making this final rule effective immediately under section 553(d) because it relieves obligations to achieve full compliance ... As such, regulated parties do not require additional time to adjust their behavior..." Also: can be justified under §553(d)(1) as "relieves a restriction."

rubrics_metrics.name: Request for public comment with specified comment period
rubrics_metrics.description: IFRs often include an explicit invitation for public comment and specify a deadline by which comments will be accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples on page: "Comments concerning this document are due no later than May 21, 2026."; "Comments must be received by April 23, 2026." Agencies set explicit comment deadlines and docket identifiers for submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency will consider and respond to comments in a subsequent final rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when issuing an IFR, agencies commonly state they will consider comments and publish a final rule responding to comments and making appropriate changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example language: "Following the close of the comment period, NHTSA will publish a final rule responding to any comments received and making any appropriate changes to the interim final rule." The IFR thus functions as a provisional regulatory text subject to later revision based on comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency may delay IFR effective date or treat IFR as proposed rule
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency can delay the effective date of an IFR and treat the IFR as a proposed rule pending issuance of a final rule that responds to comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: HUD example: "HUD is now delaying the effective date of the 2026 interim final rule until after issuance of the final rule... HUD will now treat the interim final rule as a proposed rule." Use when agency decides not to put IFR into effect immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hold public hearings and extend comment periods to promote participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may grant requests for public hearings (including virtual hearings) and extend written-comment deadlines to increase public participation in response to interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA example: "Given the public interest in these rules and to further public participation, the EPA is granting these requests and will hold the public hearings via virtual platform... In addition, the EPA is extending the deadlines for written comments..." Agencies may set separate hearing dates for different IFRs and adjust comment deadlines accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections to prior IFRs for amendatory-language, grammatical, or technical errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may publish correction documents to fix amendatory-language errors, grammatical mistakes, or other technical errors in previously published IFRs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: "issuing this document to correct the interim final rule... corrections address comments provided by the Office of the Federal Register regarding amendatory language and grammatical and technical errors..." Corrections typically identify specific page/paragraph changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt IFR as final rule or rescind IFR
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may adopt a previously issued IFR as a final rule (with or without changes) or may issue a rescission of an IFR restoring prior regulatory text or removing IFR provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: CEQ: "adopting the interim final rule published ... as final"; EPA: "is rescinding the interim final rule... and intends to address the same subject matter through notice-and-comment rulemaking culminating in a final rule." Agencies will often explain responses to comments when adopting IFRs as final.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification as a 'major rule' and Congressional Review Act (CRA) reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: IFRs may be designated a 'major rule' (OIRA/OMB determination), which triggers CRA reporting obligations and may affect timing/effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page text: "OIRA has determined that this interim final rule is a major rule... As required by the Congressional Review Act, the OCC will submit the interim final rule and other appropriate reports to Congress and the Government Accountability Office for review." Agencies note CRA compliance and any resultant procedural impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: IFR appropriate for interpretative rules, policy statements, or rules of agency organization/procedure/practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Parts of an IFR that concern interpretative rules, general statements of policy, or organizational/procedural matters may be non-substantive and therefore may justify omission of notice-and-comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example language: "Certain parts of this interim final rule concern interpretative rules, general statements of policy, or rules of agency organization, procedure, or practice. Other parts... concern minor or technical changes for which good cause exists to make notice and comment unnecessary."

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of IFR to revise compliance deadlines or make targeted temporary changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may use IFRs to revise compliance dates or make targeted temporary amendments (often accompanied by requests for comment), especially where timelines create impracticability or where immediate relief is claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: EPA revising compliance date from July 17, 2025 to January 17, 2027 and "seeks comments on this targeted revision to the compliance date and will respond and update this interim final action as appropriate." NESHAP example similarly revises compliance deadlines to address inability to comply with existing deadlines.
